analysis.one_liner: Requires companies moving jobs to low-wage countries to give workers 180 days notice plus severance, health coverage, and retraining money.
analysis.headline: Introduced with one sponsor in October 1993, the bill never left the Senate Labor Committee and died when that Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill targeted companies that close a US plant or lay off workers because the work has been shifted to a country with wages below half the US average or weaker labor standards. Those employers would have to notify workers and local governments 180 days ahead, then pay each laid-off worker a month of wages per year of service, continue health coverage for 18 months, cover retraining costs up to $10,000, and top up early-retirement pensions. Companies that skipped these duties would be barred from federal contracts for the affected products and could be sued by workers, states, and cities.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at factories with 25 or more employees who lose their jobs because the work moves overseas. They would get 180 days notice, severance pay equal to four weeks of wages per year of service, 18 months of continued health insurance, up to $10,000 for retraining and relocation, weekly bonuses while in training, and pension credits for older workers near retirement. States and cities that gave tax breaks or subsidies to a company that then shipped jobs abroad could claw that money back.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers laid off when jobs move overseas

how_it_helps.text: Employers moving work to a country where average wages are under half the US level, or where overtime, child labor, or safety standards are weaker than US law, must give affected employees 180 days written notice before closing a plant or carrying out a mass layoff [S3].

Each affected employee would receive severance of four weeks of wages multiplied by years of service, 18 months of continued group health coverage, retraining and relocation reimbursement up to $10,000, and training incentive payments worth 25 percent of a week's wages for each week in training [S3].
Workers within five years of retirement age would get pension benefits equal to what five more years of full-time service would have earned, computed at their existing pay rate [S3].
A company that fails to provide the notice or benefits is barred from federal contracts for the transferred products or closely similar ones, with a national security waiver available [S3].
Workers could sue for lost wages and benefits plus equal liquidated damages, and could bring class actions; the Labor Secretary could investigate, subpoena records, and sue on workers' behalf [S3].
States and local governments that gave a company tax relief or subsidies to keep or create jobs could recover the value of that assistance from the employer if the jobs are moved anyway [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Companies with 25 or more employees that shift work to low-wage or weak-standards countries. They would bear the notice costs, severance, 18 months of health coverage, retraining reimbursements, and pension top-ups for affected workers, and they would face lawsuits with double damages and possible exclusion from federal contracts. Compliance costs would be passed on partly in higher prices or, at the margin, taken into account when deciding whether to move jobs overseas.

drawbacks.text: The requirements would raise the cost of relocating production abroad, which critics would argue could push some companies to keep operations in the US but scale back hiring, automate instead, or raise prices [S2].

The bill applies only to a subset of closings: those tied within a year to a work transfer to a country with wages below 50 percent of the US average or substantially weaker labor standards, and employers could avoid liability by proving the foreign expansion was unrelated to the layoff, a factual question that would invite litigation [S3].

An employer could contest liability for years through the good-faith defense and court proceedings, meaning workers facing immediate income loss might not see money quickly; the bill provides no government fund to pay benefits while disputes are resolved [S3].
Only employers with 25 or more employees are covered, and part-time employees are excluded from the headcount, so workers at smaller firms and many part-timers get nothing [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers whose jobs actually move to a low-wage country, the protections are substantial: months of advance notice, meaningful severance, health coverage, and retraining money, all things workers otherwise lose overnight. The cost falls narrowly on the companies making the transfer rather than on taxpayers, which is the bill's design logic. The main honest criticisms are that it adds friction only in a defined set of cases, that liability fights could delay payments, and that it does nothing for the broader wage pressure from global competition, which the bill's own findings acknowledge. It also stacks on top of the existing WARN Act notice regime rather than replacing it.

outcome.mechanism: Senator Riegle introduced the bill in October 1993 and it was sent to the Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the 103rd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Donald Riegle (D-MI) introduced the American Jobs Protection Act on October 18, 1993, framing it as a response to jobs moving to low-wage countries and to the risks he associated with the pending NAFTA agreement [S1][S3].
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Labor and Human Resources the same day; no cosponsors signed on [S1][S4].
No further action was recorded: the committee never reported the bill, the Senate never debated it, and no vote was ever taken before the 103rd Congress ended on January 3, 1995 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers that move work to low-wage countries are better off, since no notice, severance, or benefit obligations were ever imposed. Laid-off workers and the towns that lose factories gained nothing.

for.name: Sen. Donald Riegle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gave introductory remarks on the Senate floor on October 18, 1993, arguing that job transfers to low-wage countries suppress US wages and burden dislocated workers and communities.

against.name: Senate Committee on Labor and Human Resources
against.role: Committee of referral; chaired by Sen. Edward Kennedy (D)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on October 18, 1993 and took no further action on it; it was never reported out of committee.

against.name: 0 cosponsors
against.role: Colleagues of the sponsor in the Senate
against.what_they_did: No senator joined as a cosponsor during the bill's life, leaving it a one-sponsor bill with no visible coalition to move it.

sides.party_line_note: No votes ever occurred and no cosponsors signed on, so the bill's partisan support beyond its Democratic sponsor was never tested; it was introduced by a Democrat and died in a Senate controlled by Democrats.

industries.industry: Manufacturers and other employers offshoring production
industries.note: These companies would have owed severance, 18 months of health coverage, retraining reimbursements, and pension top-ups to workers displaced when work moves to low-wage countries, plus exposure to double-damages lawsuits and federal contract bans. The bill's entire purpose was to make offshoring to low-standard countries more expensive.

industries.industry: Federal contractors in affected product lines
industries.note: A company that skipped the notice or benefit requirements could not contract with the United States to supply the transferred or substantially similar products or services, except under a national security waiver.

industries.industry: State and local governments that subsidize employers
industries.note: Governments that offered tax relief or location subsidies to keep jobs local would be able to claw back the value of that assistance when the company moved the jobs abroad anyway.
